主要内容: This article evaluates the accuracy of the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) employment, labor force, and macroeconomic projections up to 2010. It highlights that while BLS generally steered customers toward the correct industry sectors, the magnitude of the decline in manufacturing was underestimated. The article also notes that the BLS projections for nonfarm payroll employment, manufacturing employment, labor force, GDP, and unemployment rate were compared with those of other government agencies such as the Congressional Budget Office (CBO), the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), and the Energy Information Administration (EIA). The mean absolute errors for BLS projections were found to be nearly equivalent to those of other agencies, with the exception of the 2010 unemployment rate projection, where BLS assumed a rate of 4.0 percent, while other agencies expected between 4.5 percent and 5.2 percent. The article also discusses the impact of the housing bubble and bust on construction employment and the unexpected rise in oil prices due to increased global demand and the commercial viability of fracking. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) evaluated its employment, labor force, and macroeconomic projections up to 2010. The analysis indicated that the unemployment rate of 4.0 percent was likely below the Non-Accelerating Inflation Rate of Unemployment (NAIRU), suggesting it was not sustainable. Starting from the 2002–12 projections, BLS adopted a 'full employment' assumption, aligning the unemployment rate with or near NAIRU. While the 2010 projections were optimistic, BLS's errors were comparable to other agencies in 2006 and 2008. The BLS projected a slightly higher margin of error in GDP growth to 2010 due to the low unemployment rate assumption. However, BLS performed best among agencies for GDP growth projections to 2006 and 2008. The mean absolute error in GDP growth projections was nearly equivalent to other agencies. Errors in the labor force growth projections were minimal, averaging 0.1 percent, similar to those of the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) and the Energy Information Administration (EIA). Most errors stemmed from the 2010 projections due to a rapid decline in the participation rate between 2008 and 2010. The BLS employment outlook was more optimistic than that of EIA, though neither anticipated the extent of recent manufacturing declines. EIA correctly projected manufacturing employment declines for all three 10-year intervals, while BLS projected slight increases. The mean absolute error for EIA's nonfarm payroll employment projections was smaller than BLS's. BLS consistently expected faster employment growth and lower unemployment rates than EIA. A naïve model, which assumes past growth rates will persist, was used as a benchmark. BLS projections outperformed the naïve model in at least half the variables, with a p-value significant at the 5-percent level. The BLS projections process begins with population size and composition forecasts, using U.S. Census Bureau data for 136 categories, including age, race, gender, and ethnic origin. These are then converted to civilian noninstitutional population (CNIP) projections, which include all persons 16 years and older not in penal or mental institutions.
